interviewQuestions.question: What does 'serverless' actually mean?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Serverless doesn't mean there are no servers involved — it means you personally never provision one, patch its OS, or plan its capacity; the provider owns all of that entirely on your behalf. What you deploy is a function: a handler like `handleRequest(event)` that the platform packages and runs in an isolated execution environment it manages, deciding on its own how many copies run in parallel and where. Billing follows the same shift — you pay per invocation and per millisecond of actual execution time, not per server-hour a machine sat there whether or not it did useful work.

Concretely: an image-resize function configured to trigger on a file upload to storage has no listening process idling and costing money between uploads — nothing runs and nothing is billed until an event actually fires, and ten simultaneous uploads can spin up ten parallel invocations without anyone provisioning capacity for that ahead of time. Contrast this with PaaS, which still runs one long-lived process serving many requests over time — you don't manage the VM underneath it, but the process itself is always running, whereas a FaaS function is invoked fresh, or opportunistically reused, per event.

The trade I'd flag explicitly: ops work doesn't vanish, it relocates — cold-start latency, per-invocation concurrency limits, execution time caps, and a genuinely stateless model all become the new operational concerns in place of server management.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish 'no server management' from 'no servers,' and can describe the pay-per-invocation billing model with a concrete example rather than a slogan.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What serverless means

interviewQuestions.question: Why is serverless cheap for a spiky, low-traffic API but potentially expensive for a constant, high-volume one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the two billing models scale completely differently against volume, and which one wins flips depending on how much of the time a workload is actually busy. An always-on VM or container bills a flat rate for every hour it exists, whether it served a thousand requests that hour or zero — for a workload that bursts once an hour and sits idle the rest of the time, that flat rate is mostly paying for idle capacity nobody used. Serverless instead bills per invocation and per millisecond of actual execution, so an API that only runs occasionally pays only for the moments it's genuinely doing work, and the idle stretches cost nothing at all — that's exactly the shape serverless pricing is built to reward.

The same math works against serverless once traffic becomes constant and high-volume: a service handling steady load around the clock never has an idle stretch to save on, so it's paying the per-invocation premium on effectively every single request, all day, every day, with no scale-to-zero benefit ever kicking in. At that point, a fixed-rate VM sized for that steady load is simply cheaper, because its cost doesn't scale with request count the way serverless cost does — past a workload-specific crossover volume, the serverless line and the flat VM cost line cross, and the VM stays cheaper beyond it.

Concretely, modeling this: a function charging a small fee per million invocations plus per-GB-second, compared against a VM at a flat $30/month, might cross over around 5 million requests a month at 200ms average execution — below that volume serverless wins by a wide margin, above it the VM does.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the cost crossover as a real, calculable threshold tied to utilization, not just recite 'serverless is cheap' or 'serverless is expensive' as an absolute.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The cost crossover, intuitively

interviewQuestions.question: A developer writes a serverless function that caches a value in a local variable to avoid recomputing it on every call. Why might this quietly fail in production?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It fails because it depends on an assumption serverless explicitly doesn't guarantee: that the next invocation runs in the same process as this one. A function instance can be frozen and reused for a later call, or destroyed entirely between calls, and there's no guarantee any two invocations share the same underlying process — the platform decides this based on its own scaling and lifecycle logic, not anything the function author controls. Anything stored in a local variable or written to local disk may or may not survive to the next invocation, which means this caching code will sometimes work — when the platform happens to reuse the same warm instance — and sometimes silently recompute from scratch, or worse, silently return stale data if the caching logic assumed "still in memory" meant "still correct."

The practical danger is that this bug is invisible in casual testing: a developer running a few manual invocations locally or in a low-traffic dev environment will likely keep hitting the same warm instance and see the cache "working," building false confidence that ships straight into production, where real concurrent traffic spins up many parallel instances that never share that in-memory state at all. This is arguably the single most common serverless bug — treating local memory as durable because it happened to survive during testing.

The fix is to move anything that needs to persist across invocations to something genuinely external — a managed cache, a database, object storage — so correctness doesn't depend on which physical instance happens to handle a given call. A function should be written to behave identically whether it's a cold start or a warm reuse, never assuming either.

**Testing:** whether you can explain why this bug is dangerous specifically because it's intermittent and passes casual testing, not just state "serverless functions are stateless" as a fact.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The local-state trap and why it hides during testing
